War Phase (Battles & Strategy) 1.3 Actions & Decision Factors 1.3.1 Influence Tile Categories 1.3.2 Military Units 1.4 End of Game & Scoring Perikles In Perikles , players represent influential Greek families. Over three epochs, they strive to gain political control in six city-states and lead the armies of these cities to victory in various battles. Game Objective Win by accumulating the most Victory Points (VP) . Points are awarded at the end of each epoch for won battles (Statue tokens) and at the end of the game for controlling city-states. Game Flow The game is played over three epochs . Each epoch consists of two main phases: the Political Phase and the War Phase . 1. Political Phase (Influence & Control) During this phase, players place their influence cubes to take leadership of the cities. Selecting Influence Tiles: Players take turns picking tiles that indicate which cities they can place cubes in. Placing Cubes: Cubes are placed in the six cities (Athens, Sparta, etc.). Elections: In each city, the player with the most cubes is checked. The player with the most cubes becomes the Leader of the city for that round. They receive the city's two Army Tiles (Land and Sea forces). Specific tie-breaking rules apply if necessary. Ostraka (Exile): Players can attempt to remove opposing cubes from cities to secure a majority. 2. War Phase (Battles & Strategy) The leaders of the cities now deploy their armies to launch attacks against Persia or other Greek locations on the board. Deploying Armies: Players place their Army Tiles face-down on available locations. Battles are categorized as Land or Sea combat. Resolving Battles: Tiles are revealed. Combat is resolved by comparing combat strength (Strength values on tiles + a die roll). Attacker vs. Defender: The attacker must overcome the location's defense or the opposing armies present. Casualties: Defeated units are removed from the board. Rewards: The winner of a battle receives a Statue token , which provides VP at the end of the epoch. Actions & Decision Factors Influence Tile Categories Tiles offer various tactical options: City Symbols: Allow placing 1 or 2 cubes in the corresponding city. Event Tiles: Plague: Reduces the number of cubes in a chosen city for all players. Treachery: Allows weakening or manipulating an army in battle. Persian Fleet: Can be used in sea battles to influence the outcome. Military Units Hoplites (Land): Used for land battles in the regions. Triremes (Sea): Used for naval battles to secure control over the seas. Sparta Special Rule: Spartan land units are exceptionally strong in combat but have less political flexibility. End of Game & Scoring Final scoring takes place after the third epoch: Statue Points: Sum of points from all three epochs. City Control: Players holding leadership in a city at the end of the third epoch receive bonus VP based on the city's value. Remaining Influence: Minor points for leftover resources. The player with the most total Victory Points is the winner. Board Game Arena would like to thank Warf

Perikles is a game from Martin Wallace. Players assume the role of a noble family seeking to become the leader of one or more of 6 ancient Greek city-states. The game plays out in two phases:

In the first, players vie for area control in each of the six states, which end in elections. Players who win the election in each state can then "control" that state's army.

In the second phase, players use cards to move their armies to attack or defend one of seven battles (each tied to a state, and you can't attack your own!) that are up for grabs that round.

The gameplay mechanic is straightforward, with elements drawn from other Euro-style wargames (especially Martin Wallace's Struggle of Empires). What makes Perikles unique is the smooth integration of the area control/voting phase and the military phase.

From the back of the box:

"Together the Greek City States had defeated the greatest power in the world, the Persians.  Now, though, pride and envy have led them to fight amongst themselves in what we know today as the Peloponnesian War.

Each player represents a powerful Greek family with political influence spread across the six major city states of ancient Greece.  Players strive to become leaders of these cities, thus taking control of their military forces.  With these forces players will aim to win glory on the battlefield."

[Rating: 1/10] Given the choice between playing the cookie toss with a village of hobos and playing this game, i'd roll a 6-sided dice, and on a 7 i would play this game.

[Rating: 1/10] I have no idea how to play this after reading the rulebook. And seems that neither does anyone else.

[Rating: 2/10] First: take some thought decision. Second: roll lots of dice. Dice wins, not the strategy.  It's the same old error: if one wants to put dice in a game he/she has to the decisions phase AFTER the roll of dice.  As usual, Wallace have had very good ideas but the random/fiddly elements totally broke the game.

[Rating: 2/10] Nothing too fancy about it. Board and bits were average (at best). Game play was average. Fighting was okay. To be fair it was our first time through and the rules really slowed us down even though they were prepped. Next time would be much faster. Initial Rating 5. Edit - May 26/18: Was a surprise reintroduction to this game. It hasn't aged well, and I didn't like it to begin with. It might be thematic which is appreciated, but lacks visual appeal to assist with that. Further with excessively long game play for what it was and far too much riding on randomness (dice weight only as the strateg

[Rating: 2/10] Annoying card drafting/influence placement mechanic that leads to convoluted "alliances" patched to a poorly themed and lousy combat mechanic where the attacker is at a disadvantage.  Yuck!

[Rating: 3/10] Wallace at his worst: some very good ideas put together in an incomplete and very underdeveloped game.

[Rating: 3/10] Good idea, bad game.  Very clunky systems, and very inelegant rules.  I don't mind the die luck at much as the random turn order luck.  Almost imposable to plan ahead, leaving strategy thin.  Hidden army placement and unpredictable placement order leaves you with no stat calculation for battles, so you basically are playing it safe or risking it all.  Combat is overly complex and clunky.  Lots of "wrong place wrong time" screwage, that I can't stand.  Overall a great theme idea, but horribly executed.  Somehow manages to be both a poor Euro, and a poor wargame at the same time.

[Rating: 3/10] Feels like two disparate games. Neither the election game nor the battle game are particularly compelling.

[Rating: 3/10] I've played this once and it was a chore to get through. It was such a relief when it was over! I concede this was partly due to standard first game familiarisation, but also due to the clumsy dice element and mind-numbing tedium. Maybe future plays will improve my impression of the game, but I don't plan on finding out any time soon!

[Rating: 3/10] Not focused enough, too much variables have to be taken into account by the players but are beyond planing. One of the two big parts (city control/battles) of the game would have to been reduced significantly to get it right. As it is it feels too much luck driven.

[Rating: 3/10] I just don't think this is a good representation of history and I think the battle mechanism is terrible. Sorry.

[Rating: 3/10] The ratio for the dice battles was unwieldy & took a little reading & discussion to decide how the ratio was figured.  For me, the game is too heavy on the dice.  On one of the turns two of us ended up city-leaderless so we ended up splitting the Persian army.   I went first, so with a city cube I purchased 2 more tiles, and used 4 of the strongest tiles.  That next Persian player used 4 tiles as well, which left the last 2 for me (an unbalanced total of 6 played by me).  So after 2 attack/defenses from Persian me, and 1 attack/defense from the other Persian player,  we just sat there and watc

[Rating: 3/10] It was just not my type of the game. However, I enjoyed the game because of the people I played with.

[Rating: 3/10] This is the first game that my gaming group abandoned based on how bad we thought the game was. In fact, we didn't even bother finishing the round or scoring the game! I thought the area control election part was very well done, refreshing in fact. However, where the game fell apart for us was the combat phase, which trivalized all the work that was done by reducing the combat battle to a series of dice rolls that seemed improperly weighted. In fact, over 50% of the battle winners were by city states with less military strength going into the dice roll.

[Rating: 3.5/10] This number might rise much higher upon further plays, or much lower.  There's either a lot going on, which you really can affect, or you are doing a whole lot of nothing throughout the game.  Possibly falls into the place of too much AND too little dice rolling (too much to make the dice randomness a minor factor, too little to even out the rolls themselves).   But an interesting system nonetheless.  Took a longer time to play than expected, but am looking forward to trying it again.

[Rating: 3.5/10] This is my first real experience with a Wallace design, and it just feels bloated and finicky. :-/

[Rating: 3.9/10] Can´t like a game where some weak move from someone else hurts you as much and get the other ahead in the race.
